questions.prompt: State feedback \(u = -Kx\) on \(\dot{x} = Ax + Bu\) replaces the state matrix with
questions.explanation: The closed loop is \(\dot{x} = (A - BK)x\) plus whatever reference term you add later. The eigenvalues that move are those of \(A - BK\), and a reachable pair is what lets a single \(K\) put them where you ask. Keeping \(A\), replacing \(A\) by \(BK\), or flipping the sign all describe a different law.

\(A\) itself, because \(K\) only rescales the output

questions.prompt: The scalar plant is \(\dot{x} = 3x + 2u\). The gain \(K\) that places the closed-loop eigenvalue at \(-5\) is
questions.explanation: \(3 - 2K = -5\) gives \(2K = 8\), so \(K = 4\). Using \(K = 5\) subtracts 10 and lands at \(-7\). Using \(K = 3/2\) cancels the open-loop 3 and lands at 0. The sign error \(3 + 2K = -5\) asks for \(K = -4\), which is the law \(u = +4x\) rather than \(u = -Kx\).

questions.prompt: The desired poles are \(-2\) and \(-8\). In the monic polynomial \((s+2)(s+8)\), the coefficient of \(s\) is
questions.explanation: \((s+2)(s+8) = s^2 + 10s + 16\). The coefficient of \(s\) is the sum of the pole magnitudes, 10. The product 16 is the constant term. The difference \(8-2 = 6\) is neither coefficient. Leaving the polynomial unexpanded does not change the sum.

questions.prompt: A scalar plant is \(\dot{x} = a x + b u\) with \(u = -k x\). Write the closed-loop eigenvalue in the names a, b, and k.
questions.explanation: Substituting the law gives \(\dot{x} = (a - b k) x\), so the eigenvalue is \(a - bk\). The product \(bk\) is what the gain moves, and the open-loop \(a\) is still there. \(a + bk\) is the sign error from writing \(u = +kx\). \(a - k\) drops the input coefficient \(b\).

questions.prompt: In controllable companion form, \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\). For the desired polynomial \(s^2 + 7s + 12\), the gain entry on the first state is
questions.explanation: With \(u = -k_1 x_1 - k_2 x_2\), the closed-loop constant term is \(3 + k_1\) and the coefficient of \(s\) is \(1 + k_2\). Matching 12 gives \(k_1 = 9\). Matching 7 gives the other entry, \(k_2 = 6\), which is not the one asked. Reporting the desired constant term 12 leaves the open-loop 3 uncancelled.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>controllable companion matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   1</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">-3   -1</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with a 0 and a 1 on the first row.

questions.prompt: Put these pole-placement steps in the order you would do them for a single input.
questions.explanation: Without full rank there is no \(K\) that hits an arbitrary polynomial, so the rank comes first. The desired polynomial is the target, and \(A - BK\) is the polynomial you can actually shape. Matching coefficients is the solve. The last eigenvalue check catches a sign error in \(u = -Kx\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 272 164" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>state feedback around the plant</title><text x="6" y="82" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">r</text><line x1="28" y1="78" x2="52" y2="78"/><polygon points="52,78 45.6,80.7 45.6,75.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><circle cx="64" cy="78" r="12"/><text x="46" y="62" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+</text><text x="42" y="108" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−</text><line x1="76" y1="78" x2="112" y2="78"/><polygon points="112,78 105.6,80.7 105.6,75.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="112" y="56" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="154" y="82" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">P</text><line x1="196" y1="78" x2="232" y2="78"/><polygon points="232,78 225.6,80.7 225.6,75.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="236" y="82" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">y</text><line x1="224" y1="78" x2="224" y2="134"/><line x1="224" y1="134" x2="64" y2="134"/><line x1="64" y1="134" x2="64" y2="90"/><polygon points="64,90 66.7,96.4 61.3,96.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="144" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">K</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A plant block with a gain K returned and subtracted.
steps: Confirm that the controllability matrix has full rank.
Choose the closed-loop poles and write the desired monic characteristic polynomial.
Write the characteristic polynomial of A - BK with the gain entries unknown.
Match coefficients and solve the linear system for K.
Recompute the eigenvalues of A - BK and compare them with the poles you chose.

questions.prompt: A 2-state plant has eigenvalues \(+2\) and \(-4\), and its controllability matrix has rank 2. One step of this argument is wrong.
questions.explanation: Reachability is the condition under which \(K\) can move every eigenvalue, including the unstable one. The rank statement and the open-loop reading are right, and the last step is the placement fact the rank buys. The third step treats an open-loop unstable pole as immovable, which is the opposite of what full rank means.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>one mark in each half-plane</title><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="48" y2="90"/><line x1="76" y1="90" x2="180" y2="90"/><line x1="208" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="189" y1="85" x2="199" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="189" y1="95" x2="199" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="57" y1="85" x2="67" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="57" y1="95" x2="67" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: One cross in the right half-plane and one cross in the left half-plane.
steps: One open-loop eigenvalue is \(+2\), so the uncontrolled system is not asymptotically stable.
The controllability matrix has rank 2, so the pair is reachable.
State feedback cannot move an unstable eigenvalue, so every gain \(K\) leaves the closed loop unstable.
A reachable pair can place both eigenvalues of \(A - BK\) in the open left half-plane.
reasons: Full rank means K can move every eigenvalue, including the unstable one.
An open-loop pole at +2 means the closed loop is unstable for every K.
A controllability matrix of rank 2 means the input vector is zero.

questions.prompt: Ackermann's formula returns the state-feedback gain when
questions.explanation: The formula solves one row \(K\) from the desired characteristic polynomial, which is a determined system exactly for a single input of full controllability rank. Extra inputs make the gain nonunique. Stability of \(A\) is not required, and a diagonal \(A\) is a special coordinate, not the hypothesis.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>controllable companion matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   1</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">-3   -1</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with a 0 and a 1 on the first row.
options: the plant has at least two inputs
there is one input and the pair \((A, B)\) is reachable
every open-loop eigenvalue is already stable
\(A\) is diagonal, so each state is its own mode

questions.prompt: Which statements hold for \(u = -Kx\) on a reachable single-input pair?
questions.explanation: Reachability is exactly the right to assign every eigenvalue of \(A - BK\). For one input, that gain changes the denominator and leaves the zeros of \(C(sI-A)^{-1}B\) in place. \(B\) is still the input matrix; \(BK\) is the rank-one update subtracted from \(A\). An unstable open-loop eigenvalue is one of the eigenvalues you are allowed to move.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>closed-loop state matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">A-BK</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A single matrix label, A minus B K.
options: Every eigenvalue of \(A - BK\) can be assigned.
The zeros of the transfer function from the input to a fixed output stay where they were.
The matrix \(B\) is replaced by \(BK\).
A positive open-loop eigenvalue makes every choice of \(K\) unstable.

questions.prompt: A unit mass is 2, the damper coefficient is 4, and the spring coefficient is 6, so \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0.5 \end{bmatrix}\). The desired polynomial is \(s^2 + 4s + 16\). The gain entry on the position state is
questions.explanation: The input column scales both gain entries by \(0.5\). The closed-loop constant term is \(3 + 0.5 k_1\). Setting that equal to 16 gives \(k_1 = 26\). Forgetting the \(0.5\) and subtracting as if \(B\) ended in 1 produces \(16 - 3 = 13\). The coefficient of \(s\) fixes the velocity gain, \(k_2 = 4\), not the position gain. The desired natural-frequency term 16 is the polynomial coefficient, not the gain.

questions.prompt: The poles of \(A - BK\) sit where you asked, and a constant reference is added as \(u = -Kx + k_r r\). A nonzero constant error in steady state is removed by
questions.explanation: Pole placement fixes the transient of \(A - BK\). A constant reference still has to pass through the DC gain, and that gain is 1 only for a particular \(k_r\). An extra state that integrates \(r - y\) is what forces the steady error to zero when the loop is stable. A larger \(K\) moves the poles again. Deleting part of \(C\) changes what you measure, and \(D\) is a feedthrough, not an integrator.

questions.figure_alt: A plant block with a gain K returned and subtracted.
options: raising every entry of \(K\) without bound
deleting a row of \(C\)
augmenting the state with an integrator on the tracking error
setting the direct term \(D\) to 1

questions.prompt: The controllability matrix of a 2-state model has rank 1. State feedback then
questions.explanation: Each missing rank is a direction \(u\) never enters, and \(A - BK\) shares the unreachable eigenvalue with \(A\). Two entries in \(K\) do not create a new direction. The unreachable eigenvalue keeps the real part it already had. An observer gain is built from \(C\), not from this rank.

options: can still place both eigenvalues, because \(K\) has two entries
makes the unreachable mode unstable even if it started stable
is the same design as an observer gain
can move only the reachable eigenvalue; the other one stays at its open-loop value
